abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Periodontal disease is an independent risk indicator for the progression of liver fibrosis, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Emerging evidence suggests that the “oral-gut-liver axis” plays a critical role. This review aims to systematically synthesize the molecular mechanisms that may plausibly contribute to the pathogenesis of liver fibrosis via this axis and to propose a novel spatiotemporal framework to guide future research and therapeutic strategies. We propose a three-phase framework that temporally dissects the fibrogenic process into initiation, amplification, and maintenance phases—a distinction that, to our knowledge, has not been systematically applied to the oral-gut-liver axis in previous literature. This framework is proposed as a working hypothesis based on integrating current preclinical and observational evidence and is intended to guide future mechanistic and interventional studies. In the initiation phase, periodontal pathogens and their virulence factors disseminate haematogenously or via the intestinal route to the liver, where, in animal models, they have been shown to activate Toll-like receptor (TLR)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling and trigger the initial inflammatory response. In the amplification phase, hepatic inflammatory cytokines disrupt the intestinal barrier, leading to a “leaky gut” and massive endotoxin translocation into the liver, theoretically establishing a self-perpetuating positive feedback loop that may drive Kupffer cell M1 polarization and hepatic stellate cell (HSC) activation. In the maintenance phase, even after the oral trigger subsides, liver-intrinsic mechanisms—including HSC autocrine TGF-β signaling, epigenetic reprogramming, extracellular matrix crosslinking, liver sinusoidal endothelial cell capillarization, and bile acid–farnesoid X receptor (FXR)/Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5) dysregulation—are hypothesized to sustain and contribute to the aggravation of fibrosis, based largely on preclinical evidence. Despite promising preclinical and observational evidence, translation to clinical practice remains hampered by the lack of high-quality randomized controlled trials with histological reversal as a hard endpoint. Future research should integrate multi-omics analysis, organoid and humanized animal models, and rigorously designed interventional trials to validate the oral-gut-liver axis as a therapeutic target. This review provides an integrated mechanistic framework that may inform future opportunities for early prevention and multidisciplinary management of periodontal disease-associated liver fibrosis.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Periodontal disease is a chronic, infectious, and inflammatory condition driven by specific pathogens. It primarily affects the tooth-supporting tissues, including the gums, periodontal ligament, alveolar bone, and cementum. Clinical features include gum redness and swelling, bleeding on probing, periodontal pocket formation, clinical attachment loss, and progressive alveolar bone resorption. In advanced stages, the disease can lead to tooth mobility and even tooth loss. Based on lesion severity, periodontal disease is classified into two main stages: gingivitis, which is confined to the gingival tissues, and periodontitis, which involves the deeper periodontal tissues (Nocini et al., 2020; Luchian et al., 2021; Yadalam et al., 2022; Palideh et al., 2023; Higashi and Taguchi, 2025). The core pathogenesis of this disease lies in an imbalance in the host’s immune-inflammatory response to pathogenic microorganisms within the subgingival plaque biofilm, disrupting the dynamic balance between tissue destruction and repair (Luchian et al., 2021; Kozak and Pawlik, 2023; Palideh et al., 2023). Epidemiological studies show that periodontal disease is one of the most prevalent oral diseases worldwide, affecting approximately 20%–50% of adults, with some estimates exceeding 1 billion affected individuals (Amato et al., 2022; Soheili et al., 2024; Hashim et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026). In the United States, nearly half of adults aged 30 and older have periodontal disease to varying degrees, with significant racial disparities in prevalence (Fleming et al., 2025; Moreno et al., 2026). Given its high prevalence and continuing upward trend, periodontal disease has become a public health challenge that cannot be ignored (Kopić et al., 2019; Agarwal et al., 2025). This oral–systemic interaction has driven the emergence of periodontal medicine, further emphasizing the critical role of oral health in maintaining overall health (Yoshida et al., 2021; Ungureanu et al., 2023).

Liver fibrosis is a pathological reparative response to chronic liver injury. It is characterized by an imbalance between extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis and degradation, resulting in excessive accumulation of fibrous tissue. This gradually replaces normal parenchyma, distorts hepatic architecture, and impairs liver function (Delgado et al., 2021; Lucantoni et al., 2021; Li and Zhu, 2022). This pathological process can be driven by various causes, including viral hepatitis, alcohol abuse, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), autoimmune liver disease, and drug-induced liver injury (Yao et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2026). At the molecular level, persistent hepatocyte injury activates hepatic stellate cells, accompanied by the release of inflammatory cytokines, infiltration by immune cells and fibroblasts, and dysregulation of key signaling pathways, such as TGF-β, collectively driving extracellular matrix metabolic imbalance (Yin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2023; Cerrito et al., 2025). Early-stage liver fibrosis is, to some extent, reversible; however, if the underlying cause persists or intervention is delayed, the condition progresses to an irreversible stage (Zhang et al., 2016; Yin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2023). Epidemiologically, as the central pathological hub in the progression of various chronic liver diseases (CLD), liver fibrosis imposes a substantial global burden. Chronic liver disease causes approximately 2 million deaths worldwide each year, accounting for about 4% of total mortality, with fibrosis observed across a wide spectrum of etiologies including viral hepatitis, alcohol-related liver disease, and MASLD (Yamaguchi, 2026; Yang et al., 2026). Although precise prevalence data in the general population are currently lacking, multiple studies have confirmed that this condition is prevalent among patients with chronic liver disease and represents a critical pathological stage that determines prognosis, posing a substantial challenge to global public health (Zhang et al., 2022; Tsuchiya et al., 2024). If left uncontrolled, liver fibrosis leads to serious clinical consequences. Widespread deposition of fibrous tissue disrupts liver lobule structure, forming regenerative nodules and causing hemodynamic disturbances. These changes ultimately progress to cirrhosis (Iredale et al., 2017; Matsuda and Seki, 2020). The persistent fibrotic microenvironment significantly increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), serving as a critical pathological bridge between cirrhosis and malignant transformation (Nan et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2025). As functional units of the liver parenchyma are lost, the liver’s synthetic, detoxification, and metabolic functions decline comprehensively, potentially leading to life-threatening complications associated with portal hypertension, such as ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and bleeding from ruptured esophageal or gastric varices (Lee et al., 2016; Iredale et al., 2017). Furthermore, the severity of fibrosis is significantly positively correlated with the risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, and liver-related adverse events such as liver decompensation (Roskilly et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2026a; Zhou et al., 2026b).

In recent years, a growing body of evidence has shown that periodontal disease and liver fibrosis are not isolated conditions but share significant epidemiological overlaps and clinical associations. The prevalence of liver fibrosis is significantly higher among patients with periodontal disease, while patients with chronic liver disease generally have poorer oral health (Vegda et al., 2024; Joo et al., 2025). This comorbidity suggests a potentially common pathophysiological link between the two conditions. However, the mechanistic basis of this association—particularly how a localized oral inflammatory condition could remotely drive hepatic fibrogenesis—remains incompletely understood. Preclinical and observational studies show that periodontal pathogens, their toxins, and inflammatory mediators can reach the liver directly via the bloodstream; however, a more critical pathway involves the “oral-gut-liver axis” (Kuraji et al., 2021). Dysbiosis and local inflammation from periodontal disease can alter the gut microbiota, compromise intestinal barrier function, and increase translocation of enteric endotoxins, which then enter the liver via the portal vein, activate hepatic immune cells and hepatic stellate cells, and accelerate fibrosis (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang and Hua, 2026). Concurrently, periodontal disease induces systemic low-grade inflammation. This inflammatory state further exacerbates hepatic inflammation and fibrosis through pro-inflammatory factors such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang and Hua, 2026). Against this backdrop, this review aims to systematically synthesize the molecular mechanisms by which periodontal disease promotes liver fibrosis through the oral-gut-liver axis. Rather than enumerating isolated pathways, we propose an integrated three-phase framework—encompassing initiation, amplification, and maintenance—to organize the mechanistic evidence. The initiation phase covers how periodontal pathogens disseminate systemically and activate hepatic TLR/NF-κB signaling, producing initial pro-inflammatory cytokines. The amplification phase explains how these inflammatory signals disrupt intestinal barrier function, creating a “leaky gut” that increases endotoxin delivery to the liver and may promote Kupffer cell M1 polarization and hepatic stellate cell (HSC) activation, creating a self-perpetuating loop, based on evidence from animal models. The maintenance phase describes how, even after the initial oral trigger diminishes, liver-intrinsic mechanisms—including HSC autocrine TGF-β signaling, epigenetic reprogramming of pro-fibrotic genes, extracellular matrix crosslinking, liver sinusoidal endothelial cell capillarization, and bile acid–FXR/TGR5 dysregulation—may sustain the activated HSC phenotype and contribute to progressive fibrosis. This framework integrates current evidence and identifies phase-specific intervention points for future clinical translation.

It should also be noted that the mechanistic evidence reviewed in the following sections originates from three distinct levels of scientific evidence—ranging from directly demonstrated mechanisms derived from animal models or well-controlled in vitro experiments, through plausible pathways inferred from observational human studies and indirect biomarkers, to speculative models that remain to be tested experimentally. We have deliberately distinguished these levels throughout the manuscript by using precise language that reflects the strength and nature of the underlying evidence, and we have explicitly indicated where direct human evidence is lacking. This transparent stratification is intended to help readers assess confidence in each proposed mechanism and identify priority areas for future validation studies. The proposed framework is derived predominantly from preclinical mechanistic studies and clinical observational data. While these lines of evidence are convergent and compelling, they do not yet establish a direct causal chain in humans. Therefore, the mechanistic pathways and epidemiological associations discussed in the following sections should be interpreted as a plausible biological model that requires rigorous validation in future interventional studies.

While the concept of an “oral-gut-liver axis” has been recognized in previous reviews, most existing frameworks describe this axis as a non-temporal, linear sequence in which oral dysbiosis leads to alterations in the gut microbiota and endotoxin translocation, which in turn drive hepatic inflammation and fibrosis (Lyu et al., 2025). These models do not temporally distinguish the phases of fibrogenesis, nor do they differentiate early, potentially reversible, inflammation-driven activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) from the later, self-sustaining fibrotic state maintained by liver-intrinsic mechanisms (Wu et al., 2026). By contrast, our three-phase framework—encompassing initiation, amplification, and maintenance—provides a dynamic, mechanistic dissection of the fibrogenic cascade. This temporal stratification enables us to identify the critical transition point at which a reversible inflammatory response becomes an irreversible fibrotic program, elucidate how a self-perpetuating positive feedback loop between hepatic inflammation and intestinal barrier dysfunction is established and sustained, and propose phase-specific therapeutic intervention strategies not addressed by existing non-temporal models. To our knowledge, no previous review has integrated the available mechanistic evidence into such a dynamic, temporally stratified framework for periodontal disease-associated liver fibrosis.

The proposed three-phase framework is a mechanistic synthesis and working hypothesis derived from integrating currently available preclinical and observational evidence, rather than a definitively established pathogenic cascade in humans. While this framework provides a useful heuristic for organizing the complex interactions along the oral-gut-liver axis and for identifying phase-specific intervention points, it remains to be rigorously tested in future prospective studies and interventional trials. Readers are therefore encouraged to interpret the proposed model as a conceptual guide for future research, not as a proven sequence of events.

sec.title: Search strategy and evidence synthesis
sec.p: This narrative review was informed by a systematic literature search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus databases up to March 2026, without language restrictions. The search strategy combined keywords related to periodontal disease (“periodontitis,” “periodontal disease,” “Porphyromonas gingivalis”), liver fibrosis (“liver fibrosis,” “hepatic fibrosis,” “cirrhosis,” “hepatic stellate cell”), the gut–liver axis (“gut–liver axis,” “intestinal barrier,” “endotoxin,” “bile acid”), and mechanistic pathways (“TLR,” “NF-κB,” “TGF-β,” “TGR5,” “FXR”). We manually screened the reference lists of included articles and relevant reviews to identify additional studies. Given the broad, multidisciplinary nature of this topic, we used a narrative synthesis approach rather than a formal meta-analysis. We included studies that addressed mechanistic, preclinical, or clinical aspects of the association between periodontal disease and liver fibrosis via the oral–gut–liver axis. We deliberately stratified the evidence into three levels (directly demonstrated in animal/human studies, inferred from observational data, and speculative) as presented in Section 6.1, to provide readers with a transparent assessment of the strength of the underlying data. This stratification was applied during synthesis, not as a formal exclusion criterion during screening.”

sec.title: Clinical characteristics and phenotypic associations between periodontal disease and liver fibrosis: clinical foundation for the three-phase framework
sec.p: Epidemiological and clinical studies have gradually revealed a phenotypic association between periodontal disease and liver fibrosis, which is particularly pronounced in the context of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Multiple cross-sectional and cohort studies have shown a dose-response relationship between periodontal disease severity and liver fibrosis stage; this association remains partially independent even after adjustment for metabolic confounders, suggesting a biological link beyond shared risk factors.

sec.title: A dose-response relationship: epidemiological and interventional evidence linking periodontitis severity to liver fibrosis stage
sec.p: Periodontal disease and liver fibrosis are highly prevalent chronic conditions that share common risk factors and pathophysiological mechanisms. Recent epidemiological and clinical studies have shown a significant positive association between the two. Both conditions have high prevalence rates and share common pathophysiological mechanisms, including insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, and systemic inflammation (Lyu et al., 2025; Mousa et al., 2026). Several large-scale population-based cohort studies have consistently shown that the severity of periodontitis is associated with a dose-response relationship regarding the risk of liver disease. For example, the Finnish Health 2000 study, which conducted long-term follow-up of 6,165 individuals without liver disease at baseline, found that the risk ratio for severe liver disease events among patients with severe periodontitis was 3.69; this association remained significant even after fully adjusting for alcohol intake, smoking, metabolic risk factors, and socioeconomic factors (Helenius-Hietala et al., 2019). Data from the UK Biobank, based on 13 years of follow-up among approximately 500,000 participants, further confirmed that poor oral health is significantly associated with an increased risk of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) (HR = 1.42), with 19.4% of this effect mediated by metabolic pathways involving very-low-density lipoproteins, fatty acids, and triglycerides (Ye et al., 2026).

Among individuals with diagnosed liver disease, the prevalence and severity of periodontal disease are closely associated with the stage of liver fibrosis. Clinical observations show that the prevalence of periodontitis is significantly elevated in patients with cirrhosis, and the severity of periodontitis is independently associated with cirrhosis (Rinčić et al., 2025). Studies of patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) have also found a significant association between periodontitis and the stage of liver fibrosis; this association remained robust after adjusting for metabolic syndrome factors, indicating an effect beyond traditional metabolic risk factors (Alazawi et al., 2017). A 5-year follow-up study involving 341 NAFLD patients further quantified this relationship: patients with higher levels of clinical attachment loss (CAL) had an increased risk of liver fibrosis; this association was even more pronounced in the obese subgroup (Kuroe et al., 2021). Furthermore, periodontal probing depth ≥ 6 mm was significantly associated with an NAFLD fibrosis score (NFS) > 0.675, suggesting that the extent of periodontal tissue destruction may serve as a clinical indicator of liver fibrosis risk (Hiroshimaya et al., 2026). Autopsy studies have also found a positive correlation between the extent of tooth loss and the severity of liver disease, providing pathological evidence for this association (Kuraji et al., 2024). Interventional studies and natural cohort data provide indirect evidence of a causal relationship. An interventional study on periodontal treatment in patients with cirrhosis found that periodontal treatment improved Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) scores, systemic inflammatory markers, and cognitive function, while reducing endotoxin and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein levels (Bajaj et al., 2018). The U.S. Veterans Compensation Cirrhosis Cohort Study showed that patients who received regular preventive dental and periodontal maintenance services had significantly reduced risks of liver decompensation, hepatocellular carcinoma, and hospitalization, and that this protective effect was independent of other medical interventions (Bajaj et al., 2026).

Table 1 summarizes key epidemiological and interventional studies, including their populations, sample sizes, main findings, and limitations. In summary, a wealth of epidemiological, clinical staging, and interventional evidence collectively supports the view that periodontal disease is associated with the progression of liver fibrosis and may serve as a modifiable source of systemic inflammation. Its severity is clearly positively correlated with the stage of liver fibrosis, laying a solid clinical foundation for further exploration of the underlying mechanisms (Ezhilarasan, 2021; Dioguardi et al., 2025). However, these observations still cannot prove that changes in periodontal conditions will reverse or halt liver fibrosis in affected patients, highlighting the need for interventional trials targeting histological endpoints.

sec.title: Initiation phase: periodontal pathogen dissemination and hepatic TLR/NF-κB activation
sec.p: This section addresses the initiation phase of the fibrogenic cascade by examining how periodontal pathogens—particularly the red complex—disseminate from oral niches into the systemic circulation and how their components activate hepatic Toll-like receptor signaling. First, this phase establishes the microbial trigger that subsequently initiates hepatic inflammation and intestinal barrier disruption (Figure 1).

caption.p: The initiation phase of the oral-gut-liver axis: periodontal pathogen dissemination and hepatic TLR/NF-κB activation. This schematic illustrates the initial events that bridge localized periodontal inflammation to hepatic fibrogenic signaling. In the periodontium, dysbiotic subgingival biofilms, particularly the "red complex" pathogens, disrupt the epithelial barrier. Periodontal pathogens and their virulence factors disseminate systemically via two primary routes: hematogenous spread through inflamed microvasculature and intestinal translocation following disruption of the gut microbiome. Upon reaching the liver, these pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) activate Toll-like receptors 2 and 4 (TLR2/4) on Kupffer cells (KCs), hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), and hepatocytes. This triggers the MyD88-dependent pathway, leading to IκB-α phosphorylation and NF-κB nuclear translocation. The resulting transcriptional upregulation of pro-inflammatory genes represents the inflammatory output that concludes the initiation phase and primes the amplification loop.

The second section diagrams liver inflammatory responses initiated by pathogen-associated molecules via TLR2/4 and MyD88 pathway in hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, and hepatic stellate cells, resulting in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α.

sec.title: Oral colonization and systemic spread of red complex pathogens
sec.p: The core pathogenic microbial community of periodontal disease, particularly the “red complex,” represented by Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, and Treponema denticola, forms a highly synergistic biofilm within the periodontal pocket (Pretzl et al., 2017; Lafaurie et al., 2023). These Gram-negative anaerobes disrupt the periodontal tissue barrier by secreting virulence factors, thereby facilitating their dissemination from local foci into the systemic circulation (Widziolek et al., 2025). Clinical microbiological studies show that the detection rate and abundance of Red Complex bacteria in patients with severe periodontitis increase significantly with greater periodontal pocket depth and are particularly enriched at sites with probing depths ≥6 mm (Checchi et al., 2016; Nozawa et al., 2020). Primary routes of entry include increased microvascular permeability due to inflammation and transient bacteremia induced by chewing, toothbrushing, or dental procedures (Brun et al., 2020; Gualtero et al., 2023). P. gingivalis can bind to red blood cells to evade phagocytic clearance, enhancing systemic colonization (Damgaard et al., 2017). Direct evidence from animal studies confirms that P. gingivalis can migrate to the liver via the bloodstream in murine models (Ding et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2023). However, direct tracking of live periodontal pathogens from the oral cavity to the human liver has not been conclusively demonstrated, and the extent to which this hematogenous route contributes to hepatic pathology in humans remains unclear.

Beyond hematogenous spread, intestinal translocation—termed “gut-oralization” is increasingly recognized. In a mouse model, oral microbiota from patients with periodontitis, when transplanted into obese mice, have been shown to alter the gut microbiota, disrupt tight junctions, increase intestinal permeability, and promote LPS entry into the portal circulation (Wang et al., 2023). Although P. gingivalis may not be directly detected in the lower gut, it can expand IL-9+ CD4+ T cells in the small intestine, decrease microbial α-diversity, and dysregulate barrier-related genes (Sohn et al., 2022). Thus, both hematogenous and transintestinal routes represent plausible mechanisms, as hypothesized to complete the initiation phase based on preclinical observations, by delivering periodontal pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) to the liver and gut.

sec.title: Hepatic TLR/NF-κB activation: the inflammatory switch
sec.p: In vitro and animal model studies have demonstrated that once periodontal pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) reach the liver, they can activate Toll-like receptors 2 and 4 (TLR2/4) on hepatocytes, Kupffer cells (KCs), and hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) (Nagasaki et al., 2020). Whether this pathway operates identically in human livers in vivo remains to be fully established. P. gingivalis lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and lipoproteins bind to TLR2/4, triggering the MyD88-dependent pathway. In HepG2 hepatocytes, P. gingivalis LPS upregulates MyD88, increases phosphorylation of NF-κB p65 and JNK, and induces release of IL-1, IL-8, and TNF-α (Ding et al., 2019). Concurrently, gingipains activate protease-activated receptor 2 (PAR2) on HSCs, thereby stabilizing TGF-β receptor II and enhancing sensitivity to TGF-β1 (Nagasaki et al., 2020).PAR2 activation has been shown to promote hepatic stellate cell activation and collagen release in experimental liver fibrosis models (Knight et al., 2012). In animal models, periodontitis-induced liver injury is accompanied by elevated expression of TLR4, MyD88, and NF-κB (Yue et al., 2021). NF-κB serves as the core transcription factor downstream of TLR signaling. Upon IKK-mediated phosphorylation and degradation of IκB-α, NF-κB translocates to the nucleus and initiates transcription of pro-inflammatory genes, including IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α (Kiziltas, 2016; Shin et al., 2022). These cytokines not only amplify intrahepatic inflammation but also directly activate HSCs—TNF-α and IL-1β promote α-SMA and type I collagen expression in HSCs (Chen et al., 2021). In a mouse model of P. gingivalis infection combined with a high-fat diet, intrahepatic TNF-α and IL-6 were elevated, along with HSC activation markers and worsened fibrosis (Nagasaki et al., 2020). This NF-κB-driven inflammatory output, as demonstrated in preclinical models, may initiate the amplification phase by acting on distal organs, particularly the intestinal epithelium.

sec.title: Amplification phase: intestinal barrier disruption and endotoxin storm
sec.p: This phase is defined by the transition from a self-limiting inflammatory signal to a self-perpetuating fibrogenic loop. The pro-inflammatory cytokines released from the liver (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) and bacterial components circulate systemically and act on the intestinal epithelium, downregulating tight junction proteins and depleting goblet cells, thereby compromising the physical and mucosal barriers. This barrier disruption triggers a “leaky gut,” allowing massive quantities of endotoxins and bacterial products to enter the portal circulation. Once in the liver, these endotoxins activate TLR4 signaling, further amplifying Kupffer cell M1 polarization and HSC activation. This establishes a positive feedback loop: hepatic inflammation is associated with intestinal barrier dysfunction, which in turn may contribute to hepatic inflammation. Beyond endotoxin translocation, periodontal dysbiosis also disrupts gut microbial metabolism of bile acids and other metabolites, creating parallel amplification pathways that reinforce the leaky gut phenotype and sustain hepatic inflammation (Figure 2).

caption.p: The amplification phase: intestinal barrier disruption, endotoxin translocation, and the self-perpetuating fibrogenic loop. This image depicts the transition from hepatic inflammation to a systemic self-amplifying loop driven by gut-liver crosstalk. Hepatic pro-inflammatory cytokines released during the initiation phase act on the intestinal epithelium. This systemic inflammation, coupled with periodontal dysbiosis, downregulates tight junction proteins, depletes goblet cells, and impairs the intestinal mucosal barrier. The resultant “leaky gut” permits massive translocation of luminal endotoxins (LPS) and other microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) into the portal circulation. This endotoxin overload reaches the liver, where it hyperactivates TLR4/NF-κB signaling in Kupffer cells and promotes polarization toward a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype. M1-polarized KCs release additional inflammatory mediators, which in turn activate hepatic stellate cells (HSCs). This establishes a positive feedback loop: hepatic inflammation drives intestinal barrier dysfunction, which in turn fuels hepatic inflammation, thereby amplifying the fibrogenic signal. HSCs initially activate during this reversible phase.

sec.title: Periodontal inflammation-induced downregulation of intestinal tight junctions
sec.p: In vivo experiments demonstrate that in periodontitis-complicated liver disease models, colonic tight junction proteins ZO-1 and occludin are significantly downregulated, accompanied by elevated serum LPS and intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP) levels (Feng et al., 2025; Jiacheng et al., 2025). Systemic inflammation activates NF-κB signaling in intestinal epithelial cells, thereby inhibiting tight junction synthesis (Li et al., 2022; Jiacheng et al., 2025). In animal models, periodontitis reduces ZO-1 and occludin expression in the ileum or colon and decreases goblet cell numbers (Zhang et al., 2019). This structural impairment transforms the intestinal barrier from a passive defense line into an active contributor to the fibrogenic loop.

sec.title: Increased permeability is associated with endotoxin translocation and hepatic inflammatory amplification
sec.p: Leaky gut allows luminal LPS and other microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) to cross the epithelium and enter the portal venous system, reaching the liver (Zhang et al., 2025). In patients with cirrhosis, intestinal permeability increases, and intestinal-origin bacterial DNA is detectable in serum, correlating with systemic inflammation (Tyc et al., 2025). Periodontitis or oral pathogen colonization exacerbates barrier damage, promotes LPS entry, and activates KC and HSC fibrosis via hepatic TLR4 signaling in animal models (Feng et al., 2025; Jiacheng et al., 2025). Antibiotic or barrier-protectant interventions reduce serum LPS levels and alleviate liver inflammation and fibrosis (Jiacheng et al., 2025). Direct evidence in humans linking periodontitis to increased gut permeability and subsequent hepatic TLR4 activation remains limited, as most studies rely on surrogate markers such as serum LPS or I-FABP rather than direct measurements of portal endotoxin levels or hepatic TLR4 activity.

The resultant endotoxin overload directly augments the hepatic inflammatory response, closing the first half of the amplification loop. Within the liver, this amplified LPS signal drives Kupffer cell polarization toward a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype, creating a persistent inflammatory microenvironment. Periodontitis induces the accumulation of KCs, B cells, and Th17 cells in the liver, upregulating pro-inflammatory genes and activating NF-κB in B cells (Bai et al., 2022). Once activated by LPS or other PAMPs, Kupffer cells release pro-inflammatory cytokines and promote HSC activation through TLR4-dependent mechanisms and extracellular vesicles (Wang et al., 2025). In NASH models, monocyte-derived CD207+ macrophages expand and collaborate with KCs to maintain inflammation (Zhang et al., 2021). ANGPTL4, upregulated in cirrhosis, promotes KC polarization and the release of pro-inflammatory factors and enhances HSC activation via TLR4/NF-κB; interference with ANGPTL4 inhibits these processes (Zhang et al., 2021). Galectin-12 deficiency promotes KC M2 polarization, which upregulates TGF-β1 via STAT6, thereby indirectly promoting HSC myofibroblastic transformation and illustrating context-dependent effects (Lee et al., 2023). During this amplification phase, HSCs are initially activated by both direct inflammatory cytokines and amplified endotoxin signaling. This initial activation remains reversible if the inflammatory stimulus is removed, whereas the transition to a hypothesized irreversible, self-sustaining state defines the maintenance phase, although longitudinal human studies are needed to confirm this.

sec.title: Feedback regulation between changes in gut microbiota composition and disruptions in secondary bile acid metabolism
sec.p: Periodontal inflammation not only directly affects the intestinal barrier but also indirectly amplifies barrier dysfunction by altering gut microbiota composition and disrupting secondary bile acid metabolism. Gut dysbiosis is often characterized by reduced short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria and an enrichment of opportunistic pathogens, which, in turn, affects bile acid deconjugation and transformation, leading to abnormal levels of secondary bile acids (Huang et al., 2025). However, the causal direction between bile acid alterations, gut dysbiosis, and periodontal disease in human MASLD patients remains unclear, as most human studies are cross-sectional and cannot distinguish cause from consequence.

Studies in animal models and cell culture have shown that disturbances in secondary bile acid metabolism can impair intestinal barrier function. For example, the primary bile acid chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) can reduce epithelial resistance and decrease occludin expression at high concentrations. In contrast, the secondary bile acid lithocholic acid (LCA) exerts a protective effect (Sarathy et al., 2017). In models of liver fibrosis, periodontal disease is often associated with reduced fecal levels of secondary bile acids, such as LCA and DCA, and decreased FXR/TGR5 signaling activity, further weakening the intestinal barrier and exacerbating liver inflammation (Zhao et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). Intervention studies have shown that targeted modulation of bile acid metabolism can restore tight junction protein expression, improve intestinal barrier function, and alleviate liver fibrosis (Gupta et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025). Thus, the bile acid-microbiota axis constitutes a parallel amplification pathway, reinforcing the leaky gut phenotype through metabolic rather than purely inflammatory mechanisms.

sec.title: Microbial metabolites as key mediators in the oral-gut-liver axis
sec.p: Beyond the well-characterized roles of LPS and bacterial translocation, emerging evidence indicates that gut microbiota-derived metabolites—including short-chain fatty acids, indole derivatives, trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), and secondary bile acids—serve as critical signaling molecules that modulate hepatic inflammation and fibrogenesis (Lyu et al., 2025). Periodontal disease-induced gut dysbiosis alters the production of these metabolites, creating a metabolic environment that may protect against or exacerbate liver fibrosis (Simas et al., 2021).

Short-chain fatty acids, primarily acetate, propionate, and butyrate, are fermentation products of dietary fiber produced by gut commensals and play a generally protective role in liver health (Simas et al., 2021). SCFAs enhance intestinal barrier integrity by promoting tight junction protein expression, modulate immune responses via G protein-coupled receptors, and suppress hepatic inflammation through inhibition of NF-κB signaling (Simas et al., 2021). In the context of periodontal disease, P. gingivalis infection has been shown to reduce the abundance of SCFA-producing microbiota in murine models, which is associated with promoting hepatic steatosis and metabolic dysfunction. Reduced SCFA production has been identified as an important pathogenic factor in MASLD progression (Simas et al., 2021). However, whether SCFA depletion directly mediates the transition from steatosis to fibrosis in periodontitis-associated liver disease remains an active area of investigation.

Indole derivatives, including indole-3-propionic acid (IPA) and indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), are gut microbial metabolites of dietary tryptophan that exert pleiotropic effects on liver metabolism and fibrosis. IPA is lower in individuals with obesity and type 2 diabetes and exhibits hepatoprotective potential by reducing markers of hepatic stellate cell activation. Gut bacteria-produced indole activates the hepatic cytochrome P450 (CYP) eicosanoid pathway through pregnane X receptor-dependent mechanisms, thereby protecting the liver against injury and fibrosis (Zhang et al., 2025). Conversely, IPA can directly activate human hepatic stellate cells through ROS-induced JNK and p38 signaling pathways in vitro, suggesting that the role of tryptophan metabolites in liver fibrosis is context-dependent—potentially protective in the intact gut-liver axis but profibrotic under conditions of metabolic dysfunction or dysbiosis (Yuan et al., 2023). The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) has been identified as a central hub linking microbiota-derived indoles to hepatic metabolic reprogramming in MASLD. Whether periodontal dysbiosis alters the production of specific indole derivatives, and how these alterations influence hepatic fibrogenesis, warrants further investigation.

Trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) is a gut microbe-dependent metabolite generated from dietary precursors (choline, phosphatidylcholine, and L-carnitine) through sequential conversion by gut microbiota to trimethylamine (TMA) and subsequent hepatic oxidation by flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 (FMO3) (Jang et al., 2024). Chronic exposure to elevated TMAO has been associated with enhanced fibrosis propensity in multiple organ systems, including metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (Jang et al., 2024). In vitro studies have demonstrated that TMAO promotes lipid deposition and fibrosis in fatty liver cells. Mechanistically, TMAO may activate pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic signaling pathways, including TGF-β/Smad and NF-κB, although the precise molecular mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Periodontal disease, by inducing gut dysbiosis, may increase TMAO production by enriching TMA-producing bacterial taxa, thereby contributing to hepatic fibrogenesis (Lyu et al., 2025). However, direct evidence linking periodontitis-associated TMAO elevation to liver fibrosis in humans is currently limited.

Secondary bile acids, as discussed in Section 4.3, represent another critical class of microbial metabolites whose dysregulation links periodontal dysbiosis to hepatic fibrosis. Gut bacteria convert primary bile acids to secondary bile acids through deconjugation and dehydroxylation; periodontal disease-induced gut dysbiosis reduces bacterial bile salt hydrolase activity, thereby decreasing secondary bile acid production and impairing FXR/TGR5 signaling (Gupta et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2025). Secondary bile acids, such as lithocholic acid (LCA), can be hepatotoxic at high concentrations and have been implicated in the progression of liver fibrosis (Schnabl et al., 2025). The balance between protective and deleterious effects of bile acids is finely tuned and likely disrupted by periodontal inflammation.

Collectively, these microbial metabolites constitute a complex metabolic network through which periodontal dysbiosis may influence hepatic fibrogenesis. While evidence for SCFAs, indoles, TMAO, and secondary bile acids is rapidly accumulating, most data come from animal models or in vitro studies, and direct human evidence—particularly linking periodontitis-specific dysbiosis to metabolite alterations and subsequent fibrosis—remains limited. Future research should integrate metabolomic profiling with longitudinal cohort studies to clarify causal relationships and identify metabolite-based biomarkers or therapeutic targets for periodontal disease-associated liver fibrosis.

sec.title: Maintenance phase: liver-intrinsic mechanisms sustaining fibrosis
sec.p: The maintenance phase represents the transition from inflammation-driven, reversible HSC activation to a self-sustaining fibrotic state that persists even after the initial oral trigger subsides. This phase is governed by liver-intrinsic mechanisms that are hypothesized to lock the fibrotic program in place, including HSC autocrine signaling, epigenetic reprogramming, extracellular matrix (ECM) crosslinking, liver sinusoidal endothelial cell (LSEC) capillarization, and bile acid–FXR/TGR5 dysregulation. These mechanisms create a pro-fibrotic microenvironment that is no longer dependent on continuous external inflammatory inputs (Figure 3).

This schematic summarizes the key self_perpetuating pathways within the liver that render fibrosis irreversible even after the initial periodontal trigger subsides. Chronic inflammatory stimuli induce persistent epigenetic reprogramming, including DNA methylation and histone modifications at pro_fibrotic gene promoters, creating “molecular scars” that lock HSCs in an activated state. Liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) undergo capillarization—loss of fenestrae and formation of a continuous basement membrane—leading to reduced nitric oxide (NO), increased endothelin-1, exacerbated hypoxia, and portal hypertension. Deposited extracellular matrix (ECM) is crosslinked by lysyl oxidase (LOX), increasing stiffness and resistance to matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) degradation; this stiffened ECM physically impedes repair and, via integrin signaling, further activates HSCs, forming a mechanical positive feedback loop.
