sec.title: Core maintenance driver: HSC autocrine TGF-β signaling and epigenetic reprogramming
sec.p: HSCs can sustain their own activation through autocrine positive feedback loops. Activated HSCs produce large amounts of TGF-β1, which, through Smad signaling, continuously stimulates HSC activation and collagen production, independent of exogenous stimuli (Tahashi et al., 2002). Furthermore, galectin-3 released from HSCs stabilizes TGF-β receptor II, increasing cellular sensitivity to TGF-β1 and amplifying this autocrine loop (Henderson et al., 2006). Chronic inflammatory exposure induces epigenetic reprogramming of HSCs. Sustained NF-κB and TGF-β signaling lead to persistent changes in DNA methylation patterns and histone modifications at the promoters of pro-fibrotic genes (Teng and Ghoshal, 2015; Li et al., 2023). These ‘molecular scars’ are thought to lock HSCs in an activated state, based largely on in vitro and animal studies. Even after the initial LPS or cytokine stimulus is withdrawn, the epigenetic landscape maintains the fibrotic transcriptional program, which is a key reason advanced fibrosis is difficult to reverse (Zhang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2023).

sec.title: Microenvironmental reinforcement: LSEC capillarization and ECM crosslinking
sec.p: The fibrotic microenvironment itself drives maintenance. Liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) under sustained inflammatory and oxidative stress undergo capillarization—loss of fenestrae and formation of a continuous basement membrane (Wang and Liu, 2021; Wang et al., 2021). This capillarization impairs exchange of substances between sinusoidal blood and hepatocytes, exacerbating hypoxia and nutrient deprivation and further promoting HSC activation. Additionally, capillarized LSECs produce less nitric oxide (NO) and more endothelin-1, thereby increasing intrahepatic resistance and contributing to portal hypertension (Wang et al., 2021). The deposited ECM is not only excessive but also qualitatively altered. Enzymes such as lysyl oxidase (LOX) catalyze collagen crosslinking, making the ECM highly rigid and resistant to degradation by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) (Li et al., 2023). This crosslinked ECM forms a physical barrier that impairs liver function and hinders the infiltration of repair cells and therapeutic agents, creating a self-perpetuating fibrotic niche. Mechanical stiffness further activates HSCs via integrin-mediated signaling, thereby closing another positive feedback loop (Li et al., 2023).

sec.title: Metabolic maintenance: bile acid–FXR/TGR5 dysregulation
sec.p: Gut microbes generate secondary bile acids exclusively: the liver synthesizes primary bile acids, conjugates them, and secretes them into the intestine, where gut bacteria deconjugate and dehydroxylate them to form secondary bile acids such as lithocholic acid (LCA) and deoxycholic acid (DCA) (Schnabl et al., 2025). The bile acid pool composition therefore depends heavily on gut microbial community structure. Periodontal disease-induced gut dysbiosis alters this metabolic conversion, reducing protective secondary bile acids and increasing the primary-to-secondary bile acid ratio, which may contribute to hepatic inflammation and fibrosis through impaired FXR/TGR5 signaling (Gupta et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2025).

Bile acids (BAs) are important signaling molecules regulating hepatic metabolism, inflammation, and fibrosis through the nuclear receptor FXR and the membrane receptor TGR5. In MASLD/MASH, the bile acid pool composition is altered, with decreased secondary bile acids, leading to weakened FXR and TGR5 signaling and reduced anti-inflammatory protection (Gillard et al., 2022). FXR activation suppresses HSC activation by inhibiting NF-κB and downregulating pro-fibrotic mediators such as TGF-β1 (Gao et al., 2018). However, in activated HSCs, SUMOylation impairs FXR signaling, limiting its antifibrotic efficacy (Zhou et al., 2020). TGR5 exerts anti-inflammatory effects in Kupffer cells via the cAMP/PKA/CREB pathway, but its role is context-dependent. In cholestatic models, TGR5 activation in cholangiocytes promotes EMT and TGF-β1 expression, exacerbating fibrosis (Tang et al., 2026). In metabolic liver disease, TGR5 deficiency worsens steatosis but reduces fibrosis markers in some models, owing to compensatory changes in serotonin (Spatz et al., 2021). Bile acid dysregulation and gut dysbiosis form a reciprocal loop. Periodontal disease-induced gut dysbiosis has been proposed to reduce bacterial bile salt hydrolase activity, based on indirect evidence from animal models and observational human microbiome studies, thereby potentially decreasing secondary bile acid production, which may impair FXR/TGR5 signaling, further compromising intestinal barrier function and promoting continued LPS translocation, although direct human evidence for this sequence is currently limited (Gupta et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2025). This metabolic dysregulation is hypothesized to sustain hepatic inflammation and HSC activation even after the oral infection is controlled, making the bile acid axis a potential key maintenance node that warrants further investigation in human studies.

Importantly, the role of TGR5 in liver fibrosis is cell-type and etiology-dependent—a nuance with direct therapeutic implications. In Kupffer cells and hepatocytes, TGR5 activation suppresses NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling via the cAMP/PKA pathway, exerting anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects (Xiang et al., 2026). In hepatic stellate cells, TGR5 agonism inhibits activation and mitochondrial fission, further supporting an anti-fibrotic profile (Keitel and Häussinger, 2018; Ma et al., 2021). However, in cholangiocytes, TGR5 activation stimulates the cAMP/PKA/CREB axis, promoting epithelial-mesenchymal transition and TGF-β1-driven fibrosis (Tang et al., 2026). This pro-fibrotic effect has been documented in hepatolithiasis and cholestatic models, suggesting that TGR5 agonists may benefit metabolic liver diseases but may be deleterious in biliary pathologies (Tang et al., 2026). Therefore, rather than a universal “pro-fibrotic” or “anti-fibrotic” designation, TGR5 should be viewed as a context-dependent modulator whose therapeutic targeting must be guided by the underlying liver disease etiology—favoring TGR5 agonism in MASLD/MASH but exercising caution in cholestatic or biliary-predominant fibrotic conditions. This distinction is particularly relevant to the oral-gut-liver axis, where periodontal disease-associated fibrosis most commonly arises in a metabolic context, in which TGR5 agonism would be predicted to confer net benefit.

sec.title: Current challenges and future directions
sec.p: While the mechanistic pathways described above provide a coherent biological framework, the clinical evidence remains largely correlative. Definitive demonstration of causality will require prospective interventional studies with hard histologic endpoints. Nevertheless, the existing evidence is compelling enough to warrant further investigation and support interdisciplinary collaboration between dentists and hepatologists. Despite the substantial progress reviewed above in elucidating the oral-gut-liver axis as a mechanistic bridge between periodontal disease and liver fibrosis, translating these insights into clinical practice faces three interconnected categories of challenges: technical bottlenecks in mechanistic tracing, limitations in causal inference, and gaps in interventional evidence. This section synthesizes these challenges and proposes a strategic roadmap for future research.

sec.title: Distinguishing evidence levels in mechanistic pathways
sec.p: The three-phase framework proposed in this review synthesizes these evidence levels and should be regarded as a heuristic model rather than a proven pathogenic sequence. The evidence tiers presented below are intended to help readers assess the strength of the underlying data for each mechanistic step. A recurring challenge in synthesizing the oral-gut-liver axis literature is the variable quality and strength of the evidence supporting each proposed mechanism. Based on the available data, the mechanistic pathways reviewed in this article can be stratified into three broad categories by current evidence level. The strongest evidence—derived from human observational studies with consistent replication and supported by animal models—supports the epidemiological association between periodontal disease severity and liver fibrosis stage, as well as elevated systemic inflammatory markers and endotoxemia in patients with periodontitis and liver disease. Moderately supported mechanisms-–demonstrated in animal models or in vitro and consistent with human biomarker data-–include TLR/NF-κB-mediated inflammatory responses to periodontal PAMPs, intestinal tight junction protein downregulation, and cytokine-driven HSC activation. The most speculative mechanisms—which remain to be directly tested in relevant human or animal models—include the precise sequence of events linking periodontal dysbiosis to specific alterations in the bile acid pool, the direct tracking of live periodontal pathogens from the oral cavity to the human liver, and the causal role of epigenetic reprogramming in sustaining fibrosis specifically in the context of periodontal disease. We have explicitly indicated these varying levels of evidence throughout the manuscript by using language that reflects the strength and nature of the underlying data, and we highlight these distinctions in the discussions above to guide future validation studies. The most speculative mechanisms—which remain to be directly tested in relevant human or animal models—include the precise sequence of events linking periodontal dysbiosis to specific alterations in the bile acid pool, the direct tracking of live periodontal pathogens from the oral cavity to the human liver, the causal role of epigenetic reprogramming in sustaining fibrosis specifically in the context of periodontal disease, and the specific contributions of individual microbial metabolites to periodontal disease-associated hepatic fibrogenesis in humans.

sec.title: The critical evidence gap: absence of RCTs with histological reversal as a hard endpoint
sec.p: Among the three categories of challenges discussed in this section—technical bottlenecks, confounding in observational studies, and lack of interventional trials—the absence of high-quality randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with liver histological reversal as a primary endpoint constitutes the most critical barrier to clinical translation. Without such trials, periodontal treatment cannot be recommended as a standard adjunctive therapy for liver fibrosis, regardless of the mechanistic plausibility or the strength of observational associations.

Epidemiological studies have consistently revealed associations between periodontal disease severity and liver fibrosis stage (summarized in Table 1). Most evidence derives from cross-sectional or observational cohort designs that cannot establish causality (Åberg and Helenius-Hietala, 2022; Liu et al., 2026). Confounding remains a persistent threat. Factors such as age, obesity, diabetes, alcohol intake, smoking, dietary patterns, and socioeconomic status may influence both periodontitis and liver fibrosis, thereby undermining the specificity of the observed associations. Large cohorts such as the Finnish Health 2000 study and the UK Biobank have applied multivariable adjustments. Residual confounding cannot be entirely excluded. Many of these confounding factors influence the gut microbiota and intestinal barrier function independently of periodontal status (Helenius-Hietala et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026). Of the three categories of challenges discussed here—confounding, lack of RCTs, and unclear dose-response—residual confounding is arguably the most intractable, as statistical adjustment alone cannot fully address it. This suggests that future causal inference should shift from purely observational designs to genetically informed approaches, such as Mendelian randomization, which are less susceptible to confounding by lifestyle factors.

Beyond confounding, the interventional evidence base remains critically underdeveloped. The absence of histological-endpoint RCTs is the most critical evidence gap in the field and directly undermines the clinical credibility of the periodontal-liver axis hypothesis. To date, no high-quality, large-sample, multicenter randomized controlled trial has evaluated liver histological reversal as a primary endpoint following periodontal therapy. Most existing intervention studies have assessed surrogate markers such as serum ALT, non-invasive fibrosis scores, or systemic inflammatory cytokines (Kamata et al., 2022). While these markers may reflect liver inflammation or fibrosis risk, they cannot be equated with improvements in fibrosis staging as defined by liver biopsy. Animal studies consistently show that periodontal intervention reduces hepatic collagen deposition and α-SMA expression (Mester et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2022). These findings have not been translated into human histological evidence. Furthermore, several studies reporting reductions in systemic inflammatory markers did not concurrently evaluate hepatic histopathology, precluding any causal attribution of observed biomarker changes to improved liver fibrosis (Bajaj et al., 2018; Krasniqi et al., 2025).

This gap should therefore be prioritized over other research directions in the clinical translational agenda. Future RCTs should be designed with adequate statistical power, based on clinically meaningful effect sizes—for example, the 12 U/L average ALT reduction observed in the SRP group in a recent multicenter trial—and should incorporate liver biopsy or at least validated non-invasive fibrosis assessment tools as primary or co-primary endpoints (Gheorghe et al., 2021; Kamata et al., 2022; Tamaki et al., 2022). Intervention protocols must be strictly standardized, clearly defining the extent, frequency, and types of instruments used, as well as standardized adjunctive therapy protocols, to minimize performance bias. Follow-up durations should span a sufficient biological window to capture meaningful changes in fibrotic tissue remodeling.

Host genetic variation adds another layer of complexity, particularly TLR4 polymorphisms, which alter LPS responsiveness and have been associated with accelerated fibrosis in chronic hepatitis C but protective effects in NAFLD. Whether these polymorphisms modify the periodontal disease-liver fibrosis association remains unexplored. Addressing this question will require adequately powered genetic association studies that stratify patients by both periodontal status and TLR4 genotype, as well as mechanistic studies using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-differentiated hepatocytes or macrophages with defined TLR4 haplotypes. Such genetic approaches could simultaneously address confounding and causal inference. Therefore, we argue that the highest priority for future clinical research should be a rigorously designed, multicenter RCT that uses liver biopsy or validated non-invasive surrogates as co-primary endpoints, with adequate statistical power and follow-up duration to capture meaningful fibrotic remodeling.

sec.title: Technical bottlenecks: microbial tracing, multi-omics, and advanced models
sec.p: Accurately tracing the translocation of oral pathogens—particularly low-abundance red complex species—across the oral, gut, and hepatic compartments remains a formidable technical hurdle. Current 16S rRNA gene sequencing offers limited resolution at the species or strain level, making it difficult to distinguish highly homologous commensals from pathogenic strains and virtually impossible to track specific lineages across anatomical niches (Oikonomou et al., 2018). This fundamental limitation undermines definitive source tracking of oral pathogens to the liver, and without this resolution, downstream mechanistic studies risk investigating the wrong microbial targets. While metagenomic shotgun sequencing improves taxonomic granularity, host DNA contamination in low-biomass samples often confounds it, and standardized bioinformatics workflows for cross-niche source tracking remain lacking (Tilg et al., 2022). Liver tissue sampling, moreover, is invasive and impractical for longitudinal monitoring, thereby forcing most studies to rely on indirect inferences from fecal or peripheral blood samples—approaches susceptible to contamination and artifacts of transient bacteremia.

Additionally, the choice of microbial profiling technology imposes inherent limitations that require careful consideration. Metatranscriptomics, which measures the active transcriptional activity of gut microbial communities rather than mere taxonomic presence, provides a more functional view of the oral-gut-liver axis. However, it faces substantial challenges, including RNA instability, rapid degradation during sample processing, and the difficulty of depleting abundant host RNA in tissue or blood samples, which can obscure microbial signals. Furthermore, metatranscriptomic analysis is highly sensitive to sequencing depth and often requires large computational resources for accurate read mapping, particularly when distinguishing highly homologous sequences between closely related species. Metabolomics offers a direct readout of microbial functional output and host-microbiome crosstalk. Still, its application to the oral-gut-liver axis is constrained by metabolite chemical diversity, limited spectral library coverage for identifying unknown compounds, and the difficulty of assigning specific metabolites to microbial or host origin without stable isotope tracing. Most human metabolomic studies in this field have been cross-sectional, limiting causal inference regarding the relationship between specific metabolites and fibrosis progression.

More recently, spatial transcriptomics and single-cell sequencing have emerged as powerful tools to dissect tissue-level heterogeneity in the oral-gut-liver axis. Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression within the spatial architecture of liver tissue, potentially identifying fibrotic niches and their surrounding cellular ecosystems, while single-cell RNA sequencing deconvolutes cell-type-specific responses to periodontal-derived stimuli, such as activation states of individual hepatic stellate cells or Kupffer cells. However, applying these technologies to periodontal disease-associated liver fibrosis remains in its infancy. Their integration with multi-omics datasets is technically challenging, requiring sophisticated bioinformatics pipelines and substantial computational infrastructure. Moreover, the high cost of spatial and single-cell technologies limits their use in large-cohort studies, and careful study design is essential to ensure adequate statistical power to detect meaningful biological signals.

To overcome these limitations, future mechanistic investigations should prioritize developing highly sensitive, strain-resolving tracking strategies that integrate multiple orthogonal data types. These may include cultivation-independent strain-specific marker gene panels, metabolic fingerprinting, and host immune response signatures as proxies for prior exposure. Among these technical hurdles, the lack of strain-level resolution in 16S rRNA sequencing represents the most fundamental limitation. Future efforts should prioritize developing strain-resolving technologies as a prerequisite for mechanistic validation, rather than pursuing multi-omics integration in parallel without a clear hierarchical framework. Additionally, the application of organoid-based co-culture systems—combining human intestinal epithelial organoids with hepatic stellate cells or hepatocyte spheroids—offers a controlled in vitro platform to dissect the direct effects of translocated pathogens and their outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) on hepatic fibrogenic responses, circumventing the confounding variables inherent in animal models (Li et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). Humanized gnotobiotic mice, colonized with patient-derived oral or fecal microbiota, provide a complementary in vivo platform that more faithfully recapitulates species-specific host-microbe interactions (Zhao et al., 2026). These advanced model systems are not interchangeable but complementary. Organoids offer high-throughput mechanistic screening with human cellular contexts, whereas humanized mice provide whole-organism physiological integration. Future research should adopt a “tiered” approach: initial mechanistic hypotheses generated in organoid co-cultures should be subsequently validated in humanized mouse models before proceeding to human trials. This sequential strategy would optimize resource allocation and increase the translational yield of preclinical findings. Ultimately, integrating multi-omics discovery, including metagenomic, metabolomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data—with functional validation in these advanced model systems will accelerate the transition from correlation-based hypotheses to mechanistically validated pathways (Liu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026).

sec.title: Unresolved questions: intervention timing, dose-response, and patient stratification
sec.p: A third translational gap concerns the unclear dose-response relationship between the timing, frequency, and intensity of periodontal treatment and hepatic benefits. The U.S. Veterans Compensation Cirrhosis Cohort Study reported that regular preventive dental care was associated with a dose-dependent reduction in the risk of decompensation and hepatocellular carcinoma (Bajaj et al., 2026). However, observational data cannot determine the optimal treatment frequency, nor can they distinguish whether early intervention yields greater benefits than late-stage treatment. Heterogeneous intervention protocols across studies—ranging from single-episode scaling and root planing (SRP) to SRP combined with systemic antibiotics or probiotics—further limit comparability and preclude the formulation of evidence-based clinical guidelines (Gheorghe et al., 2021; Kamata et al., 2022). Critically, no study has yet defined an “effective intervention window” based on baseline fibrosis stage, leaving clinicians uncertain whether periodontal treatment should be offered to all liver disease patients or specifically targeted to those with early-stage fibrosis. The heterogeneity in treatment protocols across studies reflects not merely methodological variation but a deeper uncertainty about the biological determinants of treatment response. The optimal intervention window and frequency likely vary by the stage of liver fibrosis and the functional status of the intestinal barrier—parameters prior studies have not systematically captured. The association between periodontitis and liver fibrosis is more pronounced in patients with MASLD or MASH, particularly among those with obesity and insulin resistance. Future trials should therefore prioritize enrollment of patients with biopsy-proven or non-invasively staged MASLD/MASH who also have moderate-to-severe periodontitis. The timing of intervention requires optimization: animal models demonstrate that periodontitis exacerbates high-fat diet-induced liver fibrosis, suggesting that early periodontal treatment—initiated at the stage of steatosis may interrupt the inflammatory cascade before fibrotic remodeling becomes established (Tari et al., 2026). Combination strategies, such as SRP plus sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors or nutritional interventions, should also be explored to improve both metabolic and fibrotic outcomes synergistically. Given the molecular heterogeneity of MASLD-associated liver fibrosis, with distinct subtypes characterized by pro-fibrotic macrophage signatures and differential expression of fibrosis-related genes such as COL1A2 and EFEMP2 (Pantano et al., 2021; He et al., 2023), future trials should incorporate baseline multi-omics profiling to stratify participants. Integration of host genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic data with oral and gut metagenomic profiles can yield multidimensional biomarker panels that identify “high-response” subgroups most likely to benefit from periodontal interventions (Lv et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Pay attention to OMV load, systemic LPS levels, and the relative abundance of P. gingivalis, as these may predict treatment response. Thus, future efforts to define dose-response relationships should be embedded within stratified trial designs that account for baseline fibrosis stage and gut permeability, rather than treating all patients as a homogeneous population. Furthermore, host genetics adds complexity to patient stratification. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the human TLR4 gene—most notably TLR4 D299G and T399I—have been shown to alter receptor structure and attenuate LPS responsiveness, with estimated population frequencies of 6–10% in European populations and 2–4% in Asian populations. These polymorphisms have been associated with a reduced risk of certain inflammatory diseases but, paradoxically, with increased susceptibility to others, reflecting TLR4’s dual role in both host defense and inflammatory pathology. In the context of liver disease, the D299G polymorphism has been linked to accelerated fibrosis progression in chronic hepatitis C and to increased risk of cirrhosis in alcoholic liver disease—possibly due to impaired clearance of bacterial products and compensatory upregulation of alternative inflammatory pathways. However, studies have also reported protective associations with MASLD severity, suggesting that the net effect of TLR4 hyporesponsiveness depends on the underlying etiology and the relative contribution of LPS-driven versus sterile inflammation. Crucially, whether TLR4 polymorphisms modify the periodontal disease-liver fibrosis association has not been directly investigated. One could hypothesize that individuals with hyporesponsive TLR4 variants might be partially protected from the hepatic effects of periodontal-derived endotoxins—or that they might compensate by upregulating TLR2, thereby remaining susceptible via a different route. Addressing this question will require adequately powered genetic association studies that stratify patients by both periodontal status and TLR4 genotype, alongside mechanistic studies using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-differentiated hepatocytes or macrophages with defined TLR4 haplotypes.

sec.title: Establishing interdisciplinary oral-liver follow-up cohorts
sec.p: The successful implementation of the above priorities—RCTs with mechanistic nesting, precision stratification, and combination strategies—ultimately depends on a robust research infrastructure. We therefore advocate establishing long-term, prospective, multicenter joint oral-liver cohorts as a foundational platform. The current fragmentation of evidence arises in part from disciplinary silos between dentistry and hepatology. We advocate establishing long-term, prospective, multicenter joint oral-liver cohorts that systematically collect standardized data from both domains. Oral parameters should include the Community Periodontal Index (CPI), clinical attachment loss (CAL), P. gingivalis-specific IgG titers, and salivary microbiome profiles; hepatic parameters should encompass Fibrosis-4 index (FIB-4), NFS, liver stiffness measurement, magnetic resonance imaging-proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF), and emerging serum biomarkers such as YKL-40 and Mac-2 binding protein glycosylation isomer (Kumagai et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2021). Drawing on the successful model of the South Korean National Health Insurance Database (n=165,032), which tracked the dose-response relationship between periodontal treatment frequency and MASLD risk (Shin et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2026), such platforms can validate causal relationships while also promoting clinical pathway integration—including routine periodontal screening in MASLD management and reciprocal hepatology referral from dental clinics. Ultimately, these interdisciplinary collaborations will accelerate the public health translation of “oral-liver axis” interventions. Such platforms would not only validate causal relationships but also promote clinical pathway integration—including routine periodontal screening in MASLD management and reciprocal hepatology referral from dental clinics—ultimately accelerating the public health translation of oral-liver axis interventions.

sec.title: Potential phase-guided therapeutic opportunities: translational implications of the three-phase framework
sec.p: A central premise of the three-phase framework—and a key distinction from previous non-temporal models of the oral-gut-liver axis—is that each phase of the fibrogenic cascade is dominated by distinct molecular drivers, which in theory makes each phase susceptible to distinct intervention strategies that could be tested in future studies. Whereas previous frameworks have described a sequential pathway from oral dysbiosis to hepatic fibrosis without dissecting the temporal evolution of the fibrogenic process, our stratification explicitly distinguishes the initial inflammatory trigger, the self-amplifying gut-liver inflammatory loop, and the liver-intrinsic maintenance phase. This phase-specific logic provides a rational basis for designing multi-node therapeutic protocols that move beyond the current “one-size-fits-all” approach to periodontal-liver intervention. However, the interventions discussed below are at markedly different stages of translational readiness. To maintain consistency with the evidence-tiering approach applied throughout this review (Section 6.1), we explicitly stratify these strategies into three maturity levels: (I) clinically translatable—agents with approved indications or in advanced-phase trials for related fibrotic conditions;(II) preclinically validated—mechanisms demonstrated in animal models but lacking human proof-of-concept data;(III) conceptual/proof-of-mechanism—strategies supported by in vitro studies or mechanistic inference, requiring substantial preclinical development before clinical consideration.

Initiation phase: targeting periodontal pathogen dissemination. The priority at this stage is to prevent or minimize the systemic spread of periodontal pathogens and their virulence factors. Strategies conceptually targeting this phase include anti-P. gingivalis vaccines, topical antimicrobial photodynamic therapy, and rigorous scaling and root planing (SRP) to reduce subgingival biofilm burden. Among these, SRP is the only intervention with established clinical feasibility in patients with liver disease, with observational studies reporting improvements in MELD scores and systemic inflammatory markers following periodontal therapy (Bajaj et al., 2018). Preclinical studies have shown that passive immunization against gingipains reduces soft tissue inflammation and bacterial dissemination in animal models, although human data remain preliminary (Shin et al., 2022). The vaccine approach should therefore be classified as maturity level III. In contrast, SRP—while supported by clinical observational data—lacks RCT-level evidence for hepatic histological benefit and thus sits between levels I and II. In practical terms, SRP can be recommended as part of comprehensive dental care for patients with chronic liver disease. Still, it cannot yet be endorsed as a specific anti-fibrotic therapy. Anti-P. gingivalis vaccines and photodynamic therapy remain experimental and should not be considered for clinical application outside well-designed trials.

Amplification phase: interrupting the gut–liver inflammatory loop. During the amplification phase, the therapeutic logic shifts to breaking the self-perpetuating inflammatory loop at the gut–liver interface. Candidate strategies include intestinal barrier protectants, TLR4 antagonists, and MyD88 inhibitors that block hepatic endotoxin sensing. In animal models of periodontitis-associated liver fibrosis, MyD88 inhibitors (e.g., TJ-M2010-5) and sodium butyrate have been shown to reduce serum LPS, restore occludin and ZO-1 expression, and attenuate hepatic collagen deposition (Zhang et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2026). However, no TLR4 antagonist or MyD88 inhibitor has yet been approved for fibrosis indications, and concerns about immunosuppression and infection further hinder clinical translation. These agents should therefore be classified as maturity level II (preclinically validated). Barrier protectants such as probiotics, prebiotics, and short-chain fatty acid supplementation have entered early-phase human trials in metabolic liver disease. Still, their specific efficacy in periodontitis-associated fibrosis remains unproven. This category thus occupies an intermediate position between levels II and I—promising but requiring dedicated RCTs with histological or validated non-invasive endpoints.

Maintenance phase: reversing or halting established fibrosis. Once HSC activation has become autonomous through autocrine TGF-β signaling, epigenetic reprogramming, and ECM crosslinking, the therapeutic goal shifts to reversing or halting established fibrosis. Among the strategies conceptually relevant to this phase, FXR agonists, particularly obeticholic acid (OCA), have advanced the furthest in clinical development. OCA has been evaluated in Phase III trials for non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) with fibrosis, demonstrating histological improvement in a subset of patients, although its risk–benefit profile remains debated (Gao et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2020). Similarly, pan-PPAR agonists such as lanifibranor have shown anti-fibrotic signals in Phase IIb/III trials for MASH. These agents should be classified as maturity level I (clinically translatable) for metabolic liver fibrosis, though their application specifically to periodontitis-associated fibrosis—and their potential interaction with oral inflammation—has not been investigated. Whether periodontal disease modifies the therapeutic response to these agents remains an open question requiring dedicated subgroup analysis or mechanistic nesting studies.

By contrast, LOXL2 inhibitors (e.g., simtuzumab) have failed to meet primary endpoints in Phase II trials for bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis, while targeting LSEC capillarization through VEGF modulation or NO donors remains at the preclinical stage, supported largely by mechanistic studies in animal models (Wang and Liu, 2021; Wang et al., 2021). The bile acid–FXR/TGR5 axis, though mechanistically attractive, presents context-dependent effects: TGR5 agonism may be anti-fibrotic in MASLD/MASH but pro-fibrotic in cholestatic conditions, complicating therapeutic translation (Keitel and Häussinger, 2018; Ma et al., 2021; Spatz et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2026; Xiang et al., 2026). These strategies should be classified as maturity levels II–III, requiring further preclinical optimization and careful patient stratification before clinical testing. In summary, the three-phase framework identifies multiple theoretically actionable nodes, but their translational readiness varies widely. Clinically actionable strategies (level I) principally include FXR and PPAR agonists, which are already available for metabolic liver fibrosis, but their efficacy specifically in periodontitis-associated disease requires dedicated investigation. Preclinically validated strategies (level II), including MyD88 inhibitors, TLR4 antagonists, and barrier protectants, are mechanistically compelling but require safety and efficacy demonstration in human trials before any clinical recommendation. Conceptual strategies (level III), such as anti-gingipain vaccines and LSEC-targeted therapies, remain distant from clinical application. We emphasize that none of these strategies can currently be recommended for standard clinical care of periodontal disease-associated liver fibrosis, except for routine periodontal management as part of overall dental hygiene. The stratification proposed here is intended to guide future research prioritization: direct resources first toward level I and II strategies with the greatest potential for near-term clinical translation, while level III strategies warrant continued mechanistic exploration but should not be positioned as imminent therapeutic options. This evidence-transparent approach aligns with the broader evidence-tiering principle we have applied throughout this review and provides a realistic framework for clinicians and researchers to assess the maturity of each intervention candidate.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Periodontal disease, long viewed as a localized oral inflammatory condition, has emerged as a modifiable systemic inflammatory driver that may accelerate liver fibrosis through the interconnected oral-gut-liver axis. The pathogenic mechanisms elucidated in this review suggest a tripartite cascade: periodontal pathogens disseminate and activate hepatic TLR/NF-κB signaling; the inflammatory burden is then amplified through intestinal barrier disruption and endotoxin translocation; and finally, liver-intrinsic mechanisms take over to maintain fibrosis independently of external triggers. This three-phase framework not only integrates current evidence but also provides a rational basis for designing phase-specific, multi-node intervention protocols. Extensive epidemiological evidence demonstrating a dose-response relationship between periodontal disease severity and liver fibrosis stage reinforces the clinical significance of these mechanistic insights. However, translating these findings into clinical practice faces three interconnected challenges: technical bottlenecks in precisely tracking pathogens across anatomical niches, persistent residual confounding in observational studies that limits causal inference, and the absence of high-quality randomized controlled trials with liver histological reversal as a primary endpoint. The highest priority for future research is to establish interdisciplinary oral-liver follow-up cohorts and conduct rigorously designed multicenter trials. Deepening this interdisciplinary perspective may eventually integrate routine dental assessment and periodontal intervention into the comprehensive care of patients with chronic liver disease, potentially slowing fibrotic progression and improving long-term prognosis if ongoing and future trials confirm their efficacy. The oral-gut-liver axis thus represents not merely a scientific frontier but a tangible opportunity for multidisciplinary patient care.
